en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Book of Puzzles,
Chapter on Familiarity.
10. The Question on the Lack of Effort in Teaching the Dhamma “Venerable Nāgasena, you say:
‘The Tathāgata brought his omniscient knowledge to full maturity over the course of four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons for the sake of uplifting the great mass of humanity.’”
And again, it is said: "Having attained omniscience, his mind inclined toward inaction, not toward teaching the Dhamma.
Venerable Nāgasena, it is just as if an archer or an archer’s pupil, having practiced his craft for many days for the sake of battle, were to shrink back when a great war actually arrived.
Even so, venerable Nāgasena, after the Tathāgata had spent four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons...
And during this interval, having brought the knowledge of omniscience to maturity, you attained omniscience for the sake of rescuing the great multitude of people,

yet you hesitated to teach the Dhamma. Or rather, venerable Nāgasena, it is as if a wrestler or a wrestler’s pupil, after training in wrestling for many days, were to falter when the time for the wrestling match has arrived.
In the same way, venerable Nāgasena, the Tathāgata, having brought the knowledge of omniscience to maturity over the course of four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons,
and having attained omniscience for the sake of uplifting the great mass of people,
has now desisted from teaching the Dhamma.
"Venerable Nāgasena, did the Tathāgata retreat out of fear? Or did he retreat because of a lack of proficiency?
Or did he retreat because of weakness? Or did he retreat because of a lack of omniscience? What is the reason for this?
Pray, tell me the reason so that my doubt may be dispelled."
“If, venerable Nāgasena, the Tathāgata brought all-knowledge to maturity over the course of four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons for the sake of delivering the great mass of humanity,
then the statement that ‘his mind inclined toward inaction rather than teaching the Dhamma once he had attained all-knowledge’ is false.”
If the mind of one who has attained omniscience inclined toward inactivity rather than teaching the Dhamma,

then the statement that “the Tathāgata brought his omniscient knowledge to maturity over four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons for the sake of uplifting the great mass of people” would also be false.
“This too is a double-pronged question, profound and difficult to unravel, which has come to you; it must be resolved by you.
“Great King, the Tathāgata has brought [the world] to maturity through four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons.
Within this interval, he attained omniscient knowledge for the sake of rescuing the great mass of people. Having attained omniscience...”
He inclined his mind toward inaction rather than teaching the Dhamma;

and that was because he saw the depth, subtlety, difficulty of seeing, difficulty of understanding, delicacy, and difficulty of penetration of the Dhamma, as well as the fact that beings delight in attachment and hold firmly to the view of a self-identity, wondering, "What indeed? How indeed?"
His mind was inclined toward non-exertion rather than the teaching of the Dhamma; his intention was solely concerned with how beings might penetrate the truth.
Great King, just as a physician or surgeon, having approached a man afflicted by many diseases, thinks: "By what means or by what medicine might this disease of his be pacified?";
even so, Great King, the Tathāgata [regards] people afflicted by the diseases of all defilements... of the Dhamma.

And seeing that [the Dhamma] was profound, subtle, difficult to see, hard to understand, delicate, and difficult to penetrate, his mind inclined toward inaction rather than to teaching the Dhamma, thinking, "What indeed? How indeed?"—this was merely his mind reflecting on the capacity for penetration by sentient beings.

Great King, it is just as when a consecrated Khattiya king has gatekeepers, military commanders, courtiers, townsmen, soldiers, forces, ministers, royal counselors, and royal officials upon whom he depends.
Upon seeing people, one might think: ‘How indeed, by what means shall I win them over?

In the same way, Great King, when the Tathāgata sees the profundity, subtlety, difficulty of seeing, difficulty of awakening, delicacy, and difficulty of penetration of the Dhamma, as well as the fact that beings delight in attachment and have firmly grasped the view of a self-identity, he thinks: ‘How indeed, by what means…’
"Indeed, his mind inclined toward indolence rather than teaching the Dhamma; this was merely a mind contemplating the penetration [of the truth] by sentient beings.
Moreover, Great King, it is the natural law (dhammatā) of all Tathāgatas that they teach the Dhamma when requested by Brahmā.
But what is the reason for that?"
At that time, all those people—ascetics, wanderers, recluses, and brahmins—were devoted to Brahmā, revered Brahmā, and had Brahmā as their ultimate goal;

therefore, by bowing down to him—who was powerful, glorious, renowned, famous, supreme, and exalted—the world with its devas would bow, take refuge, and resolve itself [toward him]. It is by this [that he is so described].
And for this reason, Great King, the Tathāgatas teach the Dhamma when requested by Brahmā.

Just as, Great King, when a king or a high royal minister bows to someone and pays them honor, the rest of the people bow and pay honor to that person because they have bowed to one who is more powerful;
even so, Great King, when Brahmā has bowed to the Tathāgatas, the world with its devas will bow, for it honors those who are honored.
“Great King, the world is Brahmā; therefore, that Brahmā entreats all the Tathāgatas for a teaching of the Dhamma, and for that reason the Tathāgatas, being entreated by Brahmā, teach the Dhamma.
“It is well, venerable Nāgasena! The question has been well unraveled; the explanation is most excellent. It is so; thus do I accept it.”
The tenth question: On being free from concern regarding the teaching of the Dhamma.
